claims.text: What the image looks like Target / donut sign (bowel-in-bowel) RLQ in toddler → intussusception
claims.quote: Target / donut sign (bowel-in-bowel) RLQ in toddler Intussusception
claims.locator: Non-Trauma Ultrasound Findings, Abdomen / Pelvis table

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Ultrasound is currently the preferred means of diagnosis (easy, relatively inexpensive, safe); the characteristic finding is the target sign
claims.quote: Currently, ultrasound is the preferred means of diagnosis; it is easily done, relatively inexpensive, and safe. The characteristic finding is termed the target sign.

claims.text: Barium enema, once preferred, shows the classic coiled-spring appearance around the intussusceptum and was usually also therapeutic, but barium occasionally enters the peritoneum through an unsuspected perforation
claims.quote: Barium enema was once the preferred initial study because it revealed the classic coiled-spring appearance around the intussusceptum. In addition to being diagnostic, barium enema was also usually therapeutic; the pressure of the barium often reduced the telescoped segments. However, barium occasionally enters the peritoneum through a clinically unsuspected perforation and causes significant peritonitis.

claims.text: Suspicion must be high, particularly with atypical presentations; studies and intervention are urgent because survival and the likelihood of nonoperative reduction decrease significantly with time
claims.quote: Suspicion of the diagnosis must be high, particularly in children with atypical presentation, and studies and intervention must be performed urgently because survival and likelihood of nonoperative reduction decrease significantly with time.

claims.text: Causes Telescoping of one portion of intestine (intussusceptum) into an adjacent segment (intussuscipiens), causing obstruction and sometimes ischemia
claims.quote: Intussusception is telescoping of one portion of the intestine (intussusceptum) into an adjacent segment (intussuscipiens), causing intestinal obstruction and sometimes intestinal ischemia.

claims.text: Untreated, the telescoping segment ultimately impairs blood flow, causing ischemia, gangrene and perforation
claims.quote: The telescoping segment obstructs the intestine and, if not treated, ultimately impairs blood flow to the intussuscepting segment (see figure ), causing ischemia, gangrene, and perforation.

claims.text: Generally 6 months to 3 years of age; 70% before age 2; slight male predominance
claims.quote: Intussusception generally occurs between 6 months and 3 years of age, and 70% of cases occur before age 2 (1). There is a slight male predominance.

claims.text: Most cases are idiopathic; the most common type is ileocolic; approximately 30% have an antecedent viral illness, with peak incidence in the viral enteritis season
claims.quote: Most cases are idiopathic. The most common type of intussusception is the ileocolic type. Approximately 30% of children with intussusception have an antecedent viral illness; there is seasonal variation, and peak incidence coincides with the viral enteritis season (1).

claims.text: In approximately 25% (typically very young and older children) a lead point triggers it: polyps, lymphoma, Meckel diverticulum, IgA-associated vasculitis when purpura involve the bowel wall
claims.quote: In approximately 25% of children who have intussusception, typically very young and older children, a lead point (ie, a mass or other intestinal abnormality) triggers the telescoping (6). Examples of lead points include polyps, lymphoma, Meckel diverticulum, and immunoglobulin A–associated vasculitis when purpura involve the bowel wall.

claims.text: Symptoms Sudden, significant colicky abdominal pain recurring every 15 to 20 minutes, often with vomiting; the child appears relatively well between episodes
claims.quote: The initial symptoms of intussusception are sudden onset of significant, colicky abdominal pain that recurs every 15 to 20 minutes, often with vomiting. The child appears relatively well between episodes.

claims.text: Later: steady pain, lethargy, heme-positive stool and sometimes currant-jelly stool, a late sign that should not be waited for
claims.quote: Later, as intestinal ischemia develops, pain becomes steady, the child becomes lethargic, and mucosal hemorrhage causes heme-positive stool on rectal examination and sometimes spontaneous passage of a currant-jelly stool. The latter, however, is a late occurrence, and physicians should not wait for this symptom to occur to suspect intussusception.

claims.text: A palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass is sometimes present
claims.quote: A palpable abdominal mass, described as sausage-shaped, is sometimes present.

claims.text: Approximately 15% present without the colicky phase, appearing lethargic as if drugged
claims.quote: Approximately 15% of children present without the colicky pain phase (1). Instead, they appear lethargic, as if drugged (atypical or apathetic presentation).

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: air or contrast enema
claims.locator: Non-Trauma Ultrasound Findings, Abdomen / Pelvis table

claims.text: Confirmed ileocolic intussusception: air enema reduction (successful in > 80%), then overnight observation for occult perforation; immediate surgery if reduction fails or the intestine has perforated
claims.quote: If ileocolic intussusception is confirmed, an air enema is used for reduction, which lessens the likelihood and consequences of perforation (1). The intussusceptum can be successfully reduced this way in > 80% of children (2). If the air enema is successful, children are observed overnight to rule out occult perforation. If reduction is unsuccessful or if the intestine has perforated, immediate surgery is required.

claims.text: Ill children with peritonitis: fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, nasogastric suction and surgery; clinically stable children: imaging to confirm and treat
claims.quote: Ill children with signs of peritonitis require fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics (eg, ampicillin, plus gentamicin and clindamycin; metronidazole plus either cefotaxime or piperacillin/tazobactam), nasogastric suction, and surgery. Clinically stable children require imaging studies to confirm the diagnosis and treat the disorder.

claims.text: After nonsurgical reduction, recurrence is approximately 13% or less
claims.quote: When reduction is achieved without surgery, the recurrence rate is approximately 13% or less, depending on the nonsurgical modality used (3).
